speakers: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host, Top Traders Unplugged, hedge fund manager)
Rich Brennan (co-host, Systematic Investor, trend follower / outlier hunter)
summary: Brennan splits trend followers into four archetypes (replicators, core diversifiers, crisis risk offset, outlier hunters) and argues rule choices (breadth, vol targeting, momentum type, symmetry, speed) should follow the objective, not a universal best. A 68-market test shows 30-market subsets underperform the full book 88% of the time. Niels adds that short-term trend funds have not delivered crisis alpha in 2025.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: in a world like that, what better way to invest your money in something that does not have a clue or tries to predict where the markets are going?
claims.claim: In an unpredictable world (deglobalisation, protectionism, diverging central banks) non-predictive trend following is attractive because it needs no forecast.
claims.conditions: trend followers have been waiting for the regime shift to pay out; US policy noise currently dominates
claims.testable: no - narrative, but regime can be tested

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Btop 50 up about 48 basis points as of Tuesday. Uh down 3 1/2% only now for the year. Uh so CTA up about half a percent down 7% for the year.
claims.claim: Aug 2025 CTA industry scoreboard: BTOP50 about -3.5% YTD, CTA index -7%, trend index -8.77%, short-term traders -5.33%.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, CTA index, trend index, short-term traders index

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: MEI World is up another 2 and a half% uh this month, up 14% now, which is pretty strong um this year.
claims.claim: Equities (MSCI World +14% YTD, S&P 500 +10.8%) strongly outperform trend followers in 2025 YTD; bonds +4.7%.
claims.indicator: MSCI World, S&P 500 TR, US Agg

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the what I refer to as the stress assets tend to be sort of doing quite well
claims.claim: In the current tough environment, trend books were making money in equities, metals, meats and Bitcoin after a hard first half; trends emerged mid-year but a copper reversal hurt.
claims.testable: partly - needs trend P&L by sector

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: once you step inside, you quickly realize even that famous mantra of cutting losses short and letting profits run isn't universal amongst trend followers
claims.claim: Trend followers share systematic, non-predictive rules and participation in sustained moves, but differ in objectives so their design (smoothness, symmetry, upside) differs.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: a high sharp might be gold for a manager whose mission is to smooth a multi-asset portfolio, but for an outlier hunter, that same number might signal that the design
claims.claim: A given metric (Sharpe) means different things per strategy objective; a high Sharpe may signal an outlier-hunting design is leaving upside on the table.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: I've seen managers that might start with an outlier mindset and slowly morph into volatility targeters simply because that's what the scoreboard rewards.
claims.claim: Performance scoreboards (Sharpe, MAR, drawdown league tables) induce style drift away from a manager's original edge, eroding long-term survivability.
claims.testable: partly - track design drift in manager data

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the Andrew Debeers of the world, the replicators. Okay, their mission is simple. Track a benchmark like the SGCTA index as closely as possible.
claims.claim: Replicator archetype: 10-30 liquid markets, daily volatility targeting, often cross-sectional momentum blended in, goal is low tracking error to the SG CTA index.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: core diversifiers. So trend following here is not a standalone product. It's a satellite allocation within a larger multiasset portfolio
claims.claim: Core diversifier archetype: liquid markets, often cross-sectional momentum, emphasis on smoothness and drawdown control to lift portfolio Sharpe/MAR via diversifying returns.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: a program that lost money for three straight years but returned 80% plus in 2008 while equities collapsed
claims.claim: Crisis risk offset archetype: shorter-term trend systems or option overlays plus convex exposures (bonds in risk-off, commodities in inflation spikes); judged on crisis payoff first, smoothness second.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Outlier hunters cast the widest possible net above 100 plus markets because we know that in any given year just a few positions will deliver the outsized gains
claims.claim: Outlier hunter archetype: 100+ markets incl. small illiquid ones, pure absolute momentum, no cross-sectional overlay, because a few trades make the whole equity curve.
claims.conditions: cost of missing fat tail exceeds cost of operational complexity

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I would call pure trend. And what I mean by that is that um, and I talk about say for example someone like Don
claims.claim: A fifth archetype, 'pure trend', targets best long-term compound return using only trend models, not crisis alpha, diversification or replication; managers must prove this transparently.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: The one exception, the only universal metric that applies to all archetypes is a long-term validated real track record.
claims.claim: The only universal evaluation metric is a long, validated live track record because it shows survival across regimes; all other metrics must match the archetype's purpose.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: payoff asymmetry, skewess and contribution from top trades will always be more revealing than a point in time sharp ratio
claims.claim: Match metric to archetype: tracking error for replicators, portfolio Sharpe/correlation for core diversifiers, crisis-period CAGR/convexity for crisis offset, skew and top-trade contribution for outlier hunters.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: let's identify all the managers we're looking at in our peer group.
claims.claim: Allocator framework: classify CTA peer group by archetype, decide which archetypes the portfolio needs, then pick the best one or two in each; no single manager delivers all objectives.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: for an outlier hunter like me, that's far too narrow for me. Um my whole edge comes from giving myself as many opportunities as possible to catch the big asymmetric moves.
claims.claim: Breadth debate: 10-30 liquid markets suffice for replication, but outlier hunters need the widest feasible universe including costlier, quirkier markets, accepting higher tracking error.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Every additional market is another lottery ticket in the fat tail draw. If I only buy a handful of tickets, my odds of hitting the jackpot collapse.
claims.claim: Under-diversification raises the role of luck: running fewer markets risks missing the few that go parabolic, while a wide book accepts many unprofitable markets for a few huge winners.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: many of the people who've been around for a long time, if you look at their returns, say over a rolling 10-year period, they're not vastly different overall
claims.claim: Counterpoint: long-lived trend managers with 20-500 markets show similar rolling 10-year returns but different timing; Niels sees no evidence that 300-500 markets is better and some top outlier-camp funds trade only 20-40.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: with my say 100 markets or just just a bit less than 100 markets I have very simple strategies but if I deployed them um with less markets they'd be far less functional
claims.claim: Breadth interacts with system design: simple rules work with about 100 markets but would be less functional with fewer, so each design choice cascades.
claims.conditions: simple rules need a wide universe

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: cross-sectional momentum on the other hand ranks all your markets against each other and tilts capital towards the strongest ones trimming or dropping the weaker ones
claims.claim: Cross-sectional momentum smooths returns and controls correlation, suiting replicators and core diversifiers, but sells into strength and can cut the biggest winners; absolute momentum lets trends run.
claims.conditions: suits smoothness objectives; harms outlier capture

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: if I catch a major uptrend in crude oil and volatility doubles halfway through, a volatility targeter will cut their position by half at the very moment
claims.claim: Volatility targeting cuts positions when volatility spikes mid-trend, clipping the largest winners; equal small ATR-normalised bets at entry left alone preserve convexity.
claims.conditions: static sizing keeps winners at full size but gives noisier equity curve

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Volatility targeting works brilliantly for strategies designed to deliver stable riskadjusted returns, especially when investors have a low tolerance for draw downs.
claims.claim: Vol targeting fits mandates with a volatility budget and low drawdown tolerance; static small bets suit strategies designed to catch home runs.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we don't worry about whether the V will go from 20% rolling 12 months V to 30%. That's just the way it works, right? But we may have a cap on the overall uh value and risk
claims.claim: Most European CTAs have moved from pure vol targeting to risk targeting: no active resizing for vol changes, but a cap on overall portfolio risk.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: fund go from an annualized V of around 35 to at some point have an annualized V of like 95
claims.claim: Static small bets can balloon: one fund's annualised vol rose from about 35 to 95 as positions grew, so 'small bets' is no protection against portfolio risk surges.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: We could in fact be actually lowering our position size at a time when the trend has risen but the volume increases then the market corrects then the market goes quiet then we increase the position size.
claims.claim: Vol targeting can add risk as well as cut it: it reduces size in volatile spikes then re-increases when markets quiet, so it is a path-dependent resizing, not only a clip on winners.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: in commodity markets the most explosive moves are often on the long side during supply shocks. So like wheat in 2022, natural gas 2021.
claims.claim: Asymmetric rules: allow longs more room in commodities (supply-shock rallies) and run wider trailing stops on equity shorts (crises fall violently) to improve tail capture.
claims.direction: long commodities with looser stops; short equities with wider stops
claims.conditions: not prediction but historic speed/magnitude differences by market and direction

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I think for me asymmetry has a little bit of a taste of optimization, right? Let's be frank.
claims.claim: Skeptical view: asymmetric long/short rules risk being optimisation; identical rules across markets are arguably more robust, and allocators rarely ask this design question.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the danger with too much speed is that you can get chopped out of a long-term trend multiple times, missing the bulk of the payoff
claims.claim: Faster systems cut losses early but get whipsawed out of long trends; long-horizon systems sit through volatility to capture multi-month moves.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: when I look objectively at a trend model and I just simply apply different time frames, there is no doubt that long-term parameters work best.
claims.claim: Across lookbacks, long-term trend parameters give the best results; only crisis-offset goals justify short-term speeds, and fixed 25/50/25 speed mixes can now be replaced by dynamic optimisation.
claims.conditions: objective is max Calmar/return, not downside protection

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: The VIX doesn't always go up when markets go down. And sometimes the VIX goes up when markets go up
claims.claim: Buying VIX is an unreliable equity hedge because VIX decomposition varies; analogously short-term trend funds sold as risk mitigation were doubted.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: tanking for two days in a row, but they lose it all the next 3 days or the next 5 days.
claims.claim: Short-term trend funds did not deliver crisis alpha in April 2025 sell-off: gains from two down days were reversed, and the short-term traders index underperformed trend on a vol-adjusted basis in H2 despite choppy markets.
claims.indicator: short-term traders index vs trend index
claims.conditions: faster reversals and slippage; V-shaped moves of 3-5 days used to be capturable

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Of those 68 markets, 27 were unprofitable over the entire test period. And yet, when we ran the portfolio equal weighted across all 68 with no hindsight application, it still delivered a MAR ratio of.8.
claims.claim: 68-market outlier-hunter test (Jan 2020 to Jul 2025, 3,264 trades): 27 of 68 markets lost money but the equal-weight book earned MAR 0.8 because the tail winners swamped the losers.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Out of those 300 samples, only 35 of them achieved a mar greater than.8, eight, which is just 12% of that sample.
claims.claim: Random 30-market subsets of the 68: only 12% matched the full-book MAR, median MAR was well under 0.5, so 88% chance a narrower universe underperforms purely from market selection luck.
claims.conditions: outlier-hunting return distribution is highly skewed
claims.testable: yes - Monte Carlo of universe subsets

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the real enemy of the outlier is not volatility or drawdowns or even bad trades. It's the quiet invisible erosion of your edge through under diversification
claims.claim: Standard metrics (MAR, Sharpe, CAGR) hide survival risk from small universes; the lopsided distribution means most small portfolios underwhelm while a few are lucky.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: live cattle, all of these small markets. Rubber, all of these small markets, milk, some that might spend long periods contributing nothing like Coco did for how many years
claims.claim: Outlier hunters accept friction in small markets and long dead spells (cocoa) because one fat-tail event can outweigh years of mediocrity.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: my priority would be always invest in new markets
claims.claim: Scaling rule: when capital grows, first add new liquid markets, second increase position size, third add systems.
claims.conditions: limited by liquidity and counterparty risk; avoid off-exchange or weak-regime markets

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: I do find system diversification to me maxes out at about 10 different trend following systems.
claims.claim: Diversification across trend systems saturates at about 10; ensembles deliberately decorrelate related markets such as Brent and crude.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: I do know that any liquid market over the long term has these fat tail properties.
claims.claim: Rationale for breadth: it is unknowable where the next outlier will come from, but any liquid market shows fat tails over time.
